headline: Wreck 3548 in 118 Feet: Sea Bass to 4 Pounds, Bluefin Working the Mud Hole Lumps
subhead: A two-decade-old number still pays off, and the tuna bite on the inshore lumps is finally worth the run.
body_markdown:
Wreck number 3548, sitting in 118 feet on the eastern lip of the Klondike, has been in my book since 2009. I marked it after a mate of mine snagged bottom there chasing bluefin and came up with a piece of steel plate on his jig. Took me three trips to find the actual structure with the old sounder, and it's paid rent every July since. This week it did it again — sea bass to four pounds, mixed in with enough shorts that you had to cull hard to keep the box respectable. That's the kind of number that doesn't show up on a chartplotter unless somebody hands it to you, and I don't hand many out, but I'll tell you the depth and let you find the pile yourself: 118 feet, current running southwest at the top of the tide, jigs and bait rigs both worked once we found the exact piece.

The bigger story this week is the bluefin showing up on the Mud Hole lumps again, and not just as a rumor from the radio. We had three trips out there since Thursday, connected on two of them, which for mid-July inshore bluefin I'll take. The fish are sitting on bait balls stacked over the humps in 90 to 130 feet, the kind of structure that pushes cooler water up from below even when the surface is running warm. Surface temps off Manasquan have been pushing into the low 70s, but out past the 20-fathom curve where these lumps sit, there's still a cooler pocket underneath that's holding the bait tight. Trolling small spreader bars and cedar plugs got the strikes in the early morning hours, before the sun got high and the fish went deeper. Once that happened we switched to jigging — the green-and-white Shimano Butterfly in the 150-gram range, dropped fast through the bait and worked with a short, aggressive stroke. Fish ran 30 to 50 pounds, nothing giant, but steady enough that a half-day trip out there is worth the fuel if you time it right on an outgoing tide with the current pushing the bait against the structure.

Yellowfin have been scarcer inshore, which tracks with what I'd expect this time of year — they're still holding out past the canyon edges, and the water temperature break that usually pulls them up onto the Hudson Canyon shoulder hasn't set up clean yet. A few boats working the deeper water off the Ridge picked at them trolling ballyhoo behind Green Machines, but it wasn't consistent enough to call it a pattern. I'd rather be honest about that than send you sixty miles for a coin flip.

Mahi are starting to show on the lobster and fish pots scattered between the Mud Hole and Barnegat Ridge, which is about two weeks ahead of when I'd normally expect them to stack up. We picked off a dozen fish in the 3 to 6 pound range working pot markers in about 100 feet of water, sight-casting small white bucktails and pilchard chunks once we spotted the shadow under the buoy. This is the appetizer — the real mahi bite on the pots usually locks in through August once the warm water fully settles over that structure, but if this early push holds, we could be ahead of schedule this year. Worth working the pot lines on your way out or back from the tuna grounds; costs you nothing to slow down and look.

Sea bass overall have been solid but not spectacular across the reef network — Axel Carlson, Sea Girt Reef, and the Triple Wrecks are all holding fish, but the average size has come down some from June as the bigger fish get picked over. Squid strips and Gulp on standard sea bass rigs, fished tight to structure in 60 to 90 feet, still fills a cooler if you're willing to move when the bite slows. Blackfish season's closed this time of year in state waters, so that's not part of the conversation right now, and cod have moved off entirely — too warm, they're long gone north or holding deep on structure we're not fishing this month.

Bonito have started showing on the inshore lumps and reef edges in scattered pockets, chasing the same bait that's holding the bluefin. Small metal jigs — half-ounce to an ounce, worked fast on light tackle — will connect if you find a breaking pod, but they move fast and don't sit still like the tuna do over structure.

Looking at the week ahead: if the wind stays out of the southwest and doesn't kick up the kind of chop that shuts down the pot-hopping for mahi, I'd put my time on that early-morning tuna window on the Mud Hole lumps before the sun gets high, then work pot markers on the ride home. The bluefin pattern has legs as long as that bait stays stacked on the humps — if it slides off, which happens fast this time of year, I'd shift effort to the wreck numbers in 100 to 130 feet and lean on sea bass to fill the box while we wait for the next push of tuna bait to show.
